source: I was given some advice I now believe in. Force is all these noblemen will listen to. I must be the one bearing the whip.
I need you to trust me. All will be well, and I'll be back home soon, safe and sound. You needn't worry.
So be it, then. I wish you the best of luck.
Have a little faith in me, Ophelia.
Thanks for arranging all of this, Bernardo.
Of course, my lord. Anything.
TEMP: this is a dummy event you shouldn't see, meant to fix an error!
Ophelia! I'm already envisioning the grand title o' this event. I'm callin' it... the Unmakin' of a Lady.
Now, defendin' yerself in the heat o' battle... that's what we should live for.
Although yer a wee mite smaller than most—we might have to settle for teachin' you to be annoying rather than dangerous.
You're going to teach me to fight?
Oh, no, these blades are fer cuttin' hair an' trimmin' roses.
Yes, I'm gonna teach you how to fight!
There you go. Just take it an' feel the heft of it.
It's... heavier than I thought such a small blade could be.
Aye. They all are. Now spread yer stance wide an' bend your knees a little. Get low to the ground.
...Er. Not that low.
Ah. Sorry.
Give it a go.
Better. See? Yer already gettin' it. And don't forget: the blade goes out.
I wagered that much.
Well, look at that! Yer a natural!
Guess I picked up a bit from watching.
Always aim for the center of yer target. Don't try an' get fancy. The easiest place you can put yer blade... take it.
Now, let's try a drill, shall we?
What on earth is this?
The good Captain is teaching me how to hold a blade.
A blade? Her men just slaughtered good Danish crewmen! How can you speak to her?
Who asked yeh to come in on us, golden boy?
I killed yer crewmen because they were weak an' left their flanks undefended. If you were wise, you'd learn from me.
You're a murderer. There is nothing worth learning from you.
Ophelia, I... don't understand.
I grow tired of yer idiot antics. This ship's too god damned small. I can't wait to be rid of yeh.
Kill or be killed, boy. That's the way o' this world. Believe it or succumb to it. I care not.
I'll be in my quarters. That's right. My quarters.
I'll be there all evenin' if yeh desire a further parley, Ophelia.
Oh. Thank you, Grace.
Ah. Yeh came after all.
Apologies for Hamlet's behavior earlier.
Why're you apologizin' for him? He's the clod-headed rooster shit, not you!
Yeh seem like you've got a good head on yer shoulders. Maybe y'can lend a hand.
I desire to learn more about this vessel I'm now commandin'.
Where do yeh normally make port? An' where were you headed? An'... who're those two women travelin' with the prince?
We came from Elsinore, from the castle's dock. We were headed to London. Not anymore, of course. The two women are Hamlet's friends, Lady Rosencrantz and Lady Guildenstern.
Ah... I've heard tell of that castle. And a few legends about th'prince's father. A great ruler and a stalwart commander, I've heard.
That King is dead. His brother Claudius now rules. And Claudius was the one who killed him.
I see. So the Prince is bein' sent away so as not to prove a royal distraction.
Yes. Hamlet's health has been... off and on, as of late. He killed my father by mistake just last night.
I—oh. Ophelia. I wish I knew somethin' kind to say. Was he a good man? Did yeh love him?
I loved him dearly. But I have faith I'll meet him again.
If yer God is as kind as he looks in the paintings, then surely yeh will. So... why'd you come with young Hamlet?
Yes. Hamlet's health has been... off and on, as of late. He almost killed my father by mistake just last night.
So... why'd you come with young Hamlet?
W-well, it's... complicated. Hamlet's uncle wants him dead. He sent me to ensure Hamlet's sentence was complete upon reaching England. But we're not going to England.
But you love him. Or did, once.
Because I've loved many a man and woman in my life, an' those eyes don't lie.
Let me guess. Dark, foreign woman at the Elsinore court. Yer not a match for th'prince's rank, an' his uncle sought to make a more strategic match. Am I right?
Something like that, yes.
Better off without 'im, I say.
I only ever found use in men for stealin' their fortunes. I've never been happier than in the arms o' a beautiful woman.
In the arms of... oh.
Yer face is ridiculous right now. Don' give me that look.
Now, there's gotta be a bottle or two somewhere aroun' here... Aha!
Anyway. Fancy a drink an' a yarn while you're here?
Alternatively, yeh can go down to th'bunks an' sleep with yer idiot companions.
No, this is much improved.
What brought you all the way to Danish waters? This hardly seems like ordinary fare for you.
Bad winds, as always. We ne'er meant to come down this far south. Sometimes yeh don't get a choice.
But then we saw yer little vessel, an' opportunity rang.
At the time, I wondered why yer ship was poorly guarded. Nary a soldier aboard.
O' course, now that yeh've told me about the King's wantin' his nephew dead, it makes sense.
We were supposed to be t'executioners, I wager.
Well, you haven't killed us yet.
When that mutiny comes t'pass tomorrow, I'll let yer friends live. No bloodshed if it ain't necessary.
My thanks, Grace.
What will you do with us once we're in Ireland?
Hmm. I find myself reconsiderin'.
If yeh'd asked me before now, I'd have said-- I'll probably see what ransom I can get for the lot o' ye.
Or, if no one would pay, would've left you at th'nearest brothel in Dublin.
You'd do that? You know what would happen to us.
I've no particular kindness fer women especially.
In my position, you've got to be ruthless. The day I get soft is the day some privateer gains on us an' takes my head clean off.
I steal an' exploit everything I possibly can.
Figured I could get a pretty few coin for Hamlet alone. Maybe you too, dependin' on how much yer mother cares.
With yer father dead, I can only assume she's grievin' something fierce.
...My mother died a long time ago.
Ah. So yer an orphan like me.
Yes. My brother, Laertes, was—is—like a second father to me, though.
Has your mind changed on the subject of ransom, then?
Not for the others. But if gettin' home's in the cards for you, I'll see what I can do when we land in Dublin.
There'll be no need for that.
It's a long story. And you wouldn't believe me. So let us say only: I will travel on with you wherever you go.
Have you sailed all of these waters?
Aye. Everything in this area, an' things outside this map's boundaries.
You mean the New World?
Wah hah hah! Of course! An' a couple things you wouldn't find on any map, save for the truly good ones.
What sorts of places do you mean?
Well. Where shall I begin? How about th'time we were washed out on a strong current an' decided to visit the frozen Snelandia...
Truly? I've heard of it, but I thought that wasn't a real place.
Of course it's real! An' your people settled it!
As I said, it all began when we were washed out on a strong current with no wind fer days...
...An' that's when I realized, it wasn't another ship at all.
It wos a cliff!
Barely got out o' there wiv' both my hands an' my head attached.
I can hardly believe this is the kind of life you live.
It scarcely seems real.
Hmph. Yer sharp. You'd do well in it, too.
There's still so much I don't know about the world.
And talking to you, I realize... I may never get to see it all.
Well, perhaps between now an' Dublin, we can find a few new experiences for you.
Always more fun to show someone else th'things you love when they 'aven't done them before.
Speaking of which...
Earlier, yeh looked surprised when I said I prefer women.
I can show you a few things I almos' guarantee yeh haven't done before.
My new bunk's decidedly roomy. Danish shipwrights know how t'build comfort.
Spend the night in Grace's bed?

source: I'd like that.
My intuition's never wrong with th'ladies.
Now. How ought we to pass the time?
I don't think so, Grace.
Ah! I thought I detected interest, but my intuition failed me.
Well, I'll tell yeh what.
How about we tell stories instead? I only 'ave three livin' friends in the entire world, so for tonight, you can be my surrogate.
Happily. I could certainly tell you some interesting stories of life at court...
...I must have fallen asleep. Where has she gone?
Milady's consorting with the nobles again.
Think she relates to them better'n us salty old sharks?
Dunnah. I think she ought've killed 'em all on the spot.
She's still blue-blooded in 'er heart, no matter what she says. She's loyal to her first husband's family.
Lady O'Flaherty! May Donal rest in peace. If only he could see what she's doin' these days...
Old Donal would be in for a shock, that's for sure. He loved 'is sweet, bonny wife. But that wife is gone. The Pirate Queen took 'er place.
(I sense there's still more I can learn if I listen in a bit longer.)
(Grace hasn't called me out yet. Perhaps if I keep listening.)
I heard some of th'other men calling her the Lady of Rockfleet Castle last night. Do y'know why?
No. What's Rockfleet?
She married Sir Richard Burke three years ago today, and divorced him two years ago today.
What! Married for only one year? War har har... well, at least it was legitimate in the law's eye.
That's not all. Th'day she divorced him, she locked herself inside Rockfleet Castle, climbed to the highest window, threw it open...
An' called out the terms of her divorce!
The balls of six bulls, that one.
I'll bet she kept all 'is gold too. Isn't that right?
More'n half of it, by the time the divorce was complete, if I remember correctly.
Ruthless, wonderful, terrifying bitch that she is.
(Still nothing from Grace. A bit more should do it.)
So why're we all the way down in Danish waters, anyhow?
Didn't yeh hear about her meeting with the Queen?
Aye! I heard they're bosom friends now. Close as can be.
An' that she refused to acknowledge her as her Queen. There is no Irish queen!
Aye to that, friend.
So long as we don't attack English ships, we're in th'clear for the far future.
Any other kind o' ship is fine. Including Danish. And gold's gold no matter what flag flies over it.
Makes sense t'me.
